Intro to Machine Learning; Linear Regression Models

import pandas as pd

import numpy as np
from plotnine import ggplot, aes, geom_point, geom_smooth, geom_line, labs, scale_x_continuous, theme_minimal
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error

Music Challenge

Which popular songs from the past will be recognized by future generations, and which will fade into obscurity? The website The Pudding conducts the Music Challenge where they ask thousands of people whether they recognize hit songs from the past. We’ll look at some of the data related to the article “Defining the 90s Music Canon”.

The data set at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/song-decay-clean/refs/heads/master/src/assets/data/lollipop_chart_data_july_13.csv contains 344 songs released in the 1990s. For each song, the proportion of survey respondents who recognized the song is recorded, for both Millennial respondents and Gen Z respondents. Our goal will be to use linear regression to predict the Gen Z recognition.

We will try several different linear regression models. Save each of your models with a different name because you will compare them at the end.

  1. Read in the data and describe the Gen Z recognition variable.
music = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/song-decay-clean/refs/heads/master/src/assets/data/lollipop_chart_data_july_13.csv")
  1. Use scikit-learn to fit a linear regression model for predicting Gen Z recognition from Millennial recognition.
X = music[["mean_millennial_recognition"]]          # double brackets -> DataFrame (2-D)
y = music["mean_gen_z_recognition"]
model_music =LinearRegression()
model_music.fit(X, y)
print("intercept:", round(model_music.intercept_, 4))
print("coef:     ", model_music.coef_.round(4))
print("R²:       ", round(model_music.score(X, y), 3))
intercept: -0.0481
coef:      [0.7067]
R²:        0.797

(ggplot(music, aes(x="mean_millennial_recognition", y="mean_gen_z_recognition"))
 + geom_point(alpha=0.6)
 + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False, color="firebrick")
 + labs(x="average millennial recognition", y="mean_gen_z_recognition")
 + theme_minimal())

Categorical Predictors (FEV data)

Do non-smokers have better lungs than smokers? One measure of lung function is forced expiratory volume (FEV), the amount of air (in liters) an individual can exhale in the first second of forceful breath. Larger values of FEV are indicative of better functioning lungs. In a study, FEV was measured for a group of 654 subjects, along with whether or not they smoked and other variables.

df_fev = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kevindavisross/data301/refs/heads/main/data/FEV.csv")

df_fev

654 rows × 5 columns

1. First fit a regression model with a single predictor: Smoking status. Since this variable is categorical you need to “dummify” it before fitting the model.

# Create one dummy variable: 1 = smoker, 0 = non-smoker
smoking_dummy = pd.get_dummies(
    df_fev["Smoking status"],
    drop_first=True,
    dtype=int
)

# Fit: FEV = intercept + slope(smoking status)
model_smoking = LinearRegression().fit(
    smoking_dummy,
    df_fev["FEV"]
)
print("Intercept:", model_smoking.intercept_)
print("Smoking coefficient:", model_smoking.coef_[0])
print("R²:", model_smoking.score(smoking_dummy, df_fev["FEV"]))
Intercept: 2.5661426146010187
Smoking coefficient: 0.7107189238605222
R²: 0.06023322003569487

2. What are the predictions from this model? How could we have known that those would be the predictions? the predictions are average FEVS for those who smoke vs those who don’t.

new = pd.DataFrame({
    smoking_dummy.columns[0]: [0, 1]
})

new["Smoking status"] = ["non-smoker", "smoker"]
new["predicted_FEV"] = model_smoking.predict(new[smoking_dummy.columns])

new
smoker Smoking status predicted_FEV

5. Fit a linear regression model with two predictors: smoking status and Age (and no interaction).

# Combine smoking-status dummy and age as predictors
X = pd.concat(
    [smoking_dummy, df_fev[["Age (months)"]]],
    axis=1
)

y = df_fev["FEV"]

# Fit the model
model_smoking_age = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

print("Intercept:", model_smoking_age.intercept_)
print(pd.Series(model_smoking_age.coef_, index=X.columns))
print("R²:", model_smoking_age.score(X, y))
Intercept: 0.3681467500269182
smoker         -0.217178
Age (months)    0.019212
dtype: float64
R²: 0.575903467141671

6. Make a scatterplot of FEV versus Age, colored by smoking status, and overlay a graph of the fitted model.

fitted = df_fev.copy()

fitted["predicted_FEV"] = model_smoking_age.predict(X)

fitted = fitted.sort_values(["Smoking status", "Age (months)"])

(
    ggplot(df_fev, aes(
        x="Age (months)",
        y="FEV",
        color="Smoking status"
    ))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.6)
    + geom_line(
        fitted,
        aes(
            x="Age (months)",
            y="predicted_FEV",
            color="Smoking status"
        ),
        size=1
    )
    + labs(
        x="Age (months)",
        y="FEV"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
)

7. Fit a linear regression model with predictors smoking status, Age, and their interaction.

# Start with smoking status and age
X_interaction = pd.concat(
    [smoking_dummy, df_fev[["Age (months)"]]],
    axis=1
)

# Add the interaction: smoker dummy × age
X_interaction["smoking_age_interaction"] = (
    X_interaction[smoking_dummy.columns[0]]
    * X_interaction["Age (months)"]
)

y = df_fev["FEV"]

# Fit the interaction model
model_interaction = LinearRegression().fit(X_interaction, y)

print("Intercept:", model_interaction.intercept_)
print(pd.Series(model_interaction.coef_, index=X_interaction.columns))
print("R²:", model_interaction.score(X_interaction, y))
Intercept: 0.2594620232712441

smoking_age_interaction   -0.013110

R²: 0.5920428464352645

8. Make a scatterplot of FEV versus Age, colored by smoking status, and overlay a graph of the fitted model.

fitted_interaction = df_fev.copy()

fitted_interaction["predicted_FEV"] = model_interaction.predict(
    X_interaction
)

fitted_interaction = fitted_interaction.sort_values(
    ["Smoking status", "Age (months)"]
)

(
    ggplot(df_fev, aes(
        x="Age (months)",
        y="FEV",
        color="Smoking status"
    ))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.6)
    + geom_line(
        fitted_interaction,
        aes(
            x="Age (months)",
            y="predicted_FEV",
            color="Smoking status"
        ),
        size=1
    )
    + labs(
        x="Age (months)",
        y="FEV"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
)

9. Compare the models. Which do you think is “best”? Why? How could you investigate?

I think that the model with age and the interaction is better because it demonstrates the relationship between age and FEV and smoking and FEV. but to test if for predictions we should make a training and test dataset and compare the RMSEs. the model with the smaller RMSE is the better model.
